articles.title: Apple is finally taking the smart home seriously
articles.summary: Apple is finally revamping its smart home strategy and taking the market more seriously this time.
articles.body:
Apple ( AAPL ) has danced around making a major push into the smart home market for years, via its HomePod, HomePod mini, and Home app. But it fell shy of ever launching its own dedicated smart home hub, ceding much of the space to Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ).

That changed on Tuesday with the launch of Apple's HomeView . Sporting a 7-inch Liquid Retina Display that can sit on a counter or be mounted to a wall, the HomeView serves as Apple's biggest smart home effort to date and could help it win over a market in flux as powerful AI models enter the home .

"Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can't run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement," Counterpoint Research research director Mohit Agrawal said in a note following Apple's Welcome Home event on Tuesday.

"Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it," he added.

The HomeView takes a lot of its software design cues from the Apple Watch , complete with a series of built-in clock faces. There's a hub screen that lets you control your smart home devices, such as lights, locks, and thermostats, as well as an iPhone-like home screen where you can open apps like FaceTime or Messages.

Users can also view multiple smart camera feeds, use the HomeView's built-in camera as a vanity mirror before they head out the door, and look up things like recipes from their iPhones and then project them on the screen.

Apple is framing both its Siri AI and its privacy stance as two key benefits of the HomeView. Siri AI will allow you to control smart home devices with your voice, make FaceTime calls, and ask broad world-knowledge questions.

The company designed the HomeView to recognize six faces via its facial recognition camera. If you want to access your personal messages, calendar, and so on, you'll need your iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network as the hub so it can authenticate you.

Apple said HomeView does all of this seamlessly, allowing you to simply walk up to it and instantly see your customized home screen and app setup.

The new hardware provides users with a long-awaited Apple-built solution for controlling smart home devices. To date, customers have had to wrangle a collection of do-it-yourself options, such as using iPads as wall-mounted command centers.

HomeView changes that, with Apple noting that the device will work with existing Apple Home and Matter-compatible accessories .

articles.title: RBI’s new CAS move explained: Track FDs in multiple banks, shares & MFs in one place and why it matters
articles.summary: You invest in mutual funds, shares, ETFs, and even fixed deposits.
articles.body: You invest in mutual funds, shares, ETFs, and even fixed deposits. But tracking your investments and keeping abreast with what money lies where can be a tricky and sometimes cumbersome task.This is where the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) latest move on Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) and interoperability of account aggregators can prove to be a game-changer for you.Announced on October 7, 2026, the measures will allow SEBI-regulated depositories to include information related to deposit accounts in CAS. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said the measures would be implemented by December 31, 2026. Once operational, the move could give investors a more comprehensive view of their financial holdings in one place, alongside their stocks, mutual funds and other securities.Let’s take a look at what has been announced, how it will benefit you and what still needs clarity:What has been announced on account aggregators and CASRBI’s statement said, “With an objective to enhance customer convenience, it has been decided to implement interoperability among NBFC-Account Aggregators (NBFC-AA).”According to the central bank, this will allow customers to access and share their financial information, across different Financial Information Providers, through any NBFC-AA of their choice.“Additionally, Depositories regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India are being facilitated to include information related to bank deposit accounts in their Consolidated Account Statement (CAS) through the NBFC-AAs,” RBI said.“This will enable demat account holders to view information relating to their demat account holdings and bank deposit accounts at one place in the CAS,” it added.What is Consolidated Account Statement?As the name suggests, CAS is a single statement that brings together an investor’s transactions and holdings across demat accounts and eligible mutual fund investments.Currently, CAS consolidates transactions and holdings in an investor’s demat accounts with the National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) and Central Depository Services Limited (CDSL), as well as eligible mutual fund investments held in statement-of-account form.It consolidates the holdings linked through the investor’s PAN, making it easier to track stocks, mutual funds, bonds and other securities in one place.Mutual fund investors without a demat account can also receive consolidated statements covering eligible folios across fund houses. Bank deposit details are not currently included in CAS.How it benefits youSimply put, having bank deposits sit alongside holdings in the Consolidated Account Statement means demat account holders can see more of their money in one place, rather than checking separate statements.Experts say the proposed addition could make it easier to review how much money is held in deposits, possibly including the provision to check whether an FD has a nominee, reconcile bank interest with Form 26AS and the Annual Information Statement (AIS), and identify unfamiliar deposits that may warrant investigation.It could also help households assess how their money is distributed between market-linked investments and deposits.Let’s understand what all is expected to be consolidated:What could be visible: Alongside existing capital-market holdings - mutual funds, stocks, bonds - the statement is expected to show fixed deposit balances, bank names and term-deposit details such as principal and maturity, with account numbers masked. The precise fields are still being finalised.Which deposits? Standard retail deposits across scheduled commercial banks - fixed deposits and recurring deposits. Crucially, this only consolidates the reporting. Through the Account Aggregator framework, balances across banks can be pulled into one periodic statement via the depositories (NSDL/CDSL).“That can make it easier to get an overall picture quickly,” says Adhil Shetty, CEO of Bankbazaar.Rohit Shah, Founder & CEO, GYR Financial Planners believes that a single screen genuinely improves decision-making.“Most investors never sit down and build their full balance sheet - fixed deposits, mutual funds, stocks, bonds all sit in different places and are rarely looked at together. Bringing them into one view is exactly the gap CAS begins to close, and seeing the whole picture tends to lead to more rational choices,” he tells TOI.Explaining the rationale of the move, Adhil Shetty says, “The RBI’s aim with interoperability among NBFC Account Aggregators is to make things more convenient for customers.”Financial information can be accessed and shared through an aggregator of the customer’s choice, without piecing it together from several sources.“A customer can use any aggregator they are comfortable with to access and share financial information held across different providers, which should make the process simpler for most people. The practical details, including how consent will work and what control customers keep over their data, are likely to become clearer as the framework takes shape,” he tells TOI.The direction is a useful step towards making it easier for people to keep track of their money, he adds.What still needs clarityThe implementation timeline for the move has been set out as December 31, 2026. Financial experts expect more clarity to emerge on the processes and privacy protection.According to Adhil Shetty, the finer points, such as which deposits will be covered, what details will show and whether deposits across banks will appear together, are likely to become clearer closer to implementation.As Rohit Shah notes, the limitations matter too. This is information, not advice - a single screen doesn't make the decision for you.“The exact deposit details shown are still being finalised, and the real benefit depends on banks and aggregators coming on board and on your giving consent. Consolidating everything in one place also raises the usual data-privacy and consent questions,” he says.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Wendy's store closures may be just the beginning, analyst warns
articles.summary: Wendy’s may be on the cusp of creating a fresh wave of restaurant closures.
articles.body:
Don't be surprised if your local Wendy's soon turns off its grills for one final time.

After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's may be on the cusp of creating a fresh wave of restaurant closures.

"With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a note on Wednesday. "That said, given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system."

Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company has reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations, with more potentially on the way.

The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base.

Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills.

Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year.

There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US.

Barish estimates the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027.

The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations.

Wright officially took over as CEO on May 21, adding to the yawning list of executive turnover at the fast food chain over the past two years. He is a seasoned fast food exec who spent the previous five years fixing Potbelly as CEO. Wright's appointment marked a return to Wendy's, where he previously served in several senior leadership roles, including COO.

Wright has his work cut out for him in saving Wendy's beyond tightening up the store base count.

articles.title: Surging gas prices pushed CPI inflation to 3.7% in September. The Fed is watching.
articles.summary: Annual inflation jumped to 3.7%, accelerating from 3.4% in August and outpacing economists' expected 3.6% jump.
articles.body:
Inflation heated up to 3.7% annually last month as energy prices soared, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data.

The latest reading came in hot, accelerating from 3.4% in August and outpacing economists' expected 3.6% jump. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.6% in September from 0.4% a month earlier.

Gas prices were a particularly large driver of the jump, rising 9.1% month over month. Average prices at the pump hit a record $4.33 last month , according to AAA data, nearly $0.50 above the previous monthly record set in 2023.

Fuel oil, which millions of Americans, primarily in the Northeast, use to heat their homes, was another pain point , spiraling 15.3% from August just before the cold months set in.

"Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices and is watched more closely by Federal Reserve officials , was also hotter than expected, rising 2.6% annually, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation was unchanged from August's hotter-than-anticipated 0.3% but also came in higher than the 0.2% economists were expecting.

"Some CPI reports seem backward looking and stale, while others seem like they're foreshadowing what's to come. This one definitely feels like the latter," Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. He called the uptick in core inflation "worrying."

On a core basis, the cost of travel and leisure was a major driver of inflation. Car rental costs rose 5.4% from a month earlier, while hotels were up 2.3%. Football and soccer fans are also paying up, with the average cost of a sporting event ticket up 7.6%.

The hot readings increase the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike benchmark interest rates later this month, rather than waiting until December.

"This makes the October meeting live," Stephanie Roth, Wolfe Research chief economist, told Yahoo Finance.

Traders see close to 50-50 odds of a rate hike next month, up from less than 25% odds before the latest data was released.

Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the latest report might not be hot enough to justify a hike this month, but inflation clearly remains a problem.

"The data reinforces the view that inflation remains too persistent for the Fed to declare victory," Shah said. "More than half the CPI basket is still running at an annualized pace above 3%, highlighting the breadth of price pressures across the economy."

Claire Boston is a Senior Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title: Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
articles.summary: Individual retirement benefits will climb an average of about $70 per month, the Social Security Administration said.
articles.body: Social Security recipients will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment next year of 3.6%, one of the largest increases this decade. But advocates say it’s still unlikely to go far enough for many struggling seniors. It’s the largest adjustment since 2022, and will amount to an additional $75.15 per month on average, according to the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans. Elevated inflation continues to bedevil the U.S. economy, with rising energy and gas prices sparked by wars in Iran and Ukraine as the primary culprits. Yet even without the added cost of gas, so-called core inflation — which excludes volatile energy and food prices — has remained stuck at about 2.5%, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. For senior citizens, who are the majority of Social Security retirement benefit recipients, next year’s increase will be welcome, but it will still come up short given rising costs, said Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director. “Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Benton said. “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.” The league found in a survey that 89% of older Americans thought the cost-of-living adjustment that kicked in this year, 2.8%, was inadequate given rising costs in the economy. About 44% of seniors draw all their income from Social Security, the survey found. The annual adjustment is typically calculated using inflation data from July, August and September. But it uses an obscure inflation index that advocates say doesn’t accurately reflect seniors’ spending priorities, which include more medical and prescription drug costs, as well as a greater likelihood that they will pay rent and generally higher home energy costs. Those categories have historically outpaced headline inflation, though the rate of medical-cost increases has slowed recently. One reform proposal would index the annual adjustment to more precisely reflect seniors’ needs — but Benton said it is unlikely to be adopted until all of Social Security is overhauled. “They need Social Security benefits to cover the cost of living, and it’s just not happening,” she said.

articles.title: Stock market today: Dow gains, S&P 500, and Nasdaq decline on hot inflation data
articles.summary: Stocks wobbled as the third quarter earnings season got underway and investors digested fresh inflation data.
articles.body: Stocks were mixed on Wednesday as investors digested hotter-than-expected inflation data, and bank earnings continued to roll in.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) gained 0.2%, the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 0.4%, and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 0.7% after stocks staggered lower on Tuesday.September's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% year over year, versus 3.6% expected by economists. Higher gas and energy prices drove inflation higher, with month-over-month prices rising 0.6%, in line with estimates. Stocks attempted to recover from a global chip sell-off, with a rebound in South Korea after KOSPI index (^KS11) declined 12% over the past five days. Chip equipment maker ASML (ASML) on Wednesday posted record third quarter sales and raised its full-year outlook amid strong AI demand. Investors await Taiwan Semiconductor earnings on Thursday (TSM) for further confirmation of the AI boom. Elsewhere, the parade of financial company earnings continued with results from Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS). Bank of America stock sank 7% as a $1.2 billion regulatory penalty and a slowdown in its Wall Street machine dented lending income. Meanwhile, BlackRock (BLK) shares rose after third quarter earnings beat analyst expectations. The reports follow several investment banking earnings reports on Tuesday, indicating that consumers are holding up despite higher interest rates, among other signals.Brent crude futures (BZ=F), the global benchmark, remained above $105 per barrel as Houthis continued to bomb Saudi Arabian energy facilities.

articles.title: Social Security announces 3.6% COLA for 2027, the highest in 4 years
articles.summary: The Social Security Administration announced the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027. Is it enough?
articles.body:
The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027. That's well above both this year's COLA and the 2.6% average over the past two decades.

Starting in January, the increase will add an average of $75 per month for roughly 75 million retired seniors and disabled workers.

The 2027 COLA will be the highest in four years — but still not enough for millions of retirees to keep up with rising food, energy, and healthcare costs .

The COLA is "supposed to offset inflation, but it under-measures it," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance. "Thanks to the war in Iran and the tariffs, we've got raging inflation and the COLA, as important as it is, will not fully offset the inflation seniors are experiencing."

The annual cost-of-living adjustment is many retirees' only source of retirement income that is not subject to inflation risk. That inflation protection is crucial because Social Security is also the largest source of income for many retirees.

Today, for about half of seniors, their monthly Social Security benefit provides at least 50% of their income, and for about 1 in 4, it's at least 90%.

For more than a quarter, it's their only source of income. The average retiree's benefit is $2,087.52 per month and will rise to $2,162.67.

The COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for urban workers, or CPI-W, which weights the costs of goods and services paid by the urban segment of the population more than other expense categories. It averages data for July, August, and September, then compares that figure with the same period last year.

Inflation heated up to 3.7% annually last month as energy prices soared, new data showed, driven primarily by higher energy prices.

Critics argue that the index does not accurately reflect the expenses many seniors face.

One proposal would use the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, to calculate COLAs. CPI-E expenditures are weighted differently, with medical care, housing, and recreation costs making up a larger share of the index than food, apparel, transportation, and education costs.

"The CPI-E is designed around the spending patterns of older Americans" and "can provide a more realistic measure of the inflation they experience," said Shannon Benton, executive director of the Senior Citizens League, a nonprofit advocacy organization.

articles.title: Netflix to cut about 6% of worldwide staff
articles.summary: Netflix is eliminating about 1,000 jobs in a round of layoffs, according to a source with knowledge of the matter.
articles.body: Netflix is eliminating about 6% of its employee roster, or roughly 1,000 jobs, in a round of layoffs announced internally Wednesday, according to a source with knowledge of the matter and a company email seen by NBC News. “Our mission — to entertain the world — is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” Netflix co-chief executives Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos said in the email to staff members Wednesday. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The source with knowledge of the matter confirmed the newspaper’s reporting was accurate. Netflix remains one of the titans of streaming, but it has struggled to boost user engagement on the platform. The service’s users watched more than 97 billion hours of content in the first half of 2026, an increase of 2% year over year, according to the company’s most recent quarterly earnings report. “Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” Sarandos said at Bloomberg’s annual media conference late last month. Netflix is expected to report its third-quarter financial results Tuesday. The majority of the job cuts will be concentrated in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and human resources teams. Peters and Sarandos said the streaming firm will “continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas” while also “making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees and investors.” In recent months, Netflix has looked for ways to boost subscriber engagement, including adding live sports programming and video podcasts licensed from third-party companies such as Bill Simmons’ The Ringer. Netflix’s layoffs come as other major Hollywood studios look to reduce costs and streamline operations. The Walt Disney Co. has cut hundreds of jobs this year under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, according to a source familiar with the matter. David Ellison’s Skydance is widely expected to shrink its workforce across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.

articles.title: Social Security COLA set to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027
articles.summary: Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent in 2027, the Trump administration announced Wednesday. With the latest cost of living adjustment (COLA), Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). Last year’s COLA was 2.8 percent. The COLA applies to the nearly 72…
articles.body:
Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent in 2027, the Trump administration announced Wednesday.

With the latest cost of living adjustment (COLA), Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). Last year’s COLA was 2.8 percent.

The COLA applies to the nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries, who received an average benefit of nearly $1,942 in August, the SSA reported .

It will also take effect for the 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), 2.5 million of whom also receive Social Security benefits. The average SSI payment was about $738 in August, per the SSA.

The SSA released its COLA for 2027 after the Bureau of Labor Statistics released inflation data for September, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI). Annual inflation was 3.7 percent in September , up from 3.4 percent in August , according to the CPI.

Frank Bisignano, the commissioner of the SSA, said the COLA will give beneficiaries “greater financial stability,” as inflation has remained above 2 percent for five-plus years.

The adjustment from the SSA is tied with 2011’s increase of 3.6 percent for the fifth-highest COLA since 1991. It was also in line with what officials at the AARP anticipated.

“We’re expecting about 3.6 percent,” Bill Sweeney, AARP’s senior vice president of government affairs, said Tuesday on NewsNation’s “The Hill.”

“That would be … about $75 a month for most people or about $900 over the course of a year,” he added Tuesday.

The Senior Citizens League also projected a 3.5 percent COLA for next year.

Roughly three-quarters of adults ages 50 and older who responded to a recent AARP survey said an adjustment of 3.5 percent would not keep up with rising prices. Instead, about 7 in 10 respondents said an increase of between 5 percent and 8 percent would be sufficient.

Earlier this year, Bisignano and other Trump administration officials projected that Social Security’s Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will be able to cover the entirety of scheduled benefits only until the fourth quarter of 2032.

At that point, the OASI fund will only be able to cover 78 percent of benefits.

Officials from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) referenced the looming deadline on Wednesday, saying the impending cut “could wipe out the previous nine years’ worth of COLAs” in 2032.

“To help restore Social Security solvency, lawmakers should consider reforming future COLAs,” the CRFB said in a statement , noting the SSA could follow the chained CPI instead of the baseline CPI.

Annual inflation, as measured by the chained CPI , was 3.5 percent in September. Chained CPI inflation consistently runs below baseline CPI inflation.

CRFB officials also proposed capping adjusted benefits for those who receive the most from the SSA. The COLA for 2027 will boost benefits for the “very richest” recipients by more than $2,200, the committee noted.

Despite the administration’s warnings, Bisignano said Monday that Social Security, a nine-decade-old program, will be around for the foreseeable future.

“It’s 90 years old. It’ll be around for another 90 years,” Bisignano said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

articles.title: Netflix to cut roughly 1,000 employees in biggest workforce reduction since 2022
articles.summary: Netflix is set to cut 6% of its staff in the company's largest round of job eliminations since 2022.
articles.body:
Netflix ( NFLX ) said Wednesday that it will cut 6% of its workforce, or about 1,000 employees, marking the company's largest reduction of employees since 2022.

The move comes as Netflix has faced a slowdown in growth over the past several quarters. The cuts will occur across the company's global operations, with a focus on Netflix's product, HR, tech, and legal departments, per an email to employees from co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters.

Netflix stock initially climbed roughly 0.3% Wednesday morning on the report, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal, before reversing to a loss of roughly 0.5%.

The stock has fallen roughly 40% over the past year as investors and analysts have evaluated struggles in both growth and engagement at the company

Netflix will "continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas" while "making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees and investors," Sarandos and Peters said in their email to employees.

The company joins streaming competitor Disney ( DIS ) in announcing large-scale layoffs in recent months.

Netflix will report earnings next week, with analysts expecting cost savings to be a major focus for Sarandos and Peters. While earnings per share of $0.80 slightly edged out estimates of $0.79 per share in the second quarter, revenue of $12.56 billion underperformed the $12.58 billion expected by Wall Street.

Critically, FX-neutral revenue growth is projected to slow in the third quarter to 11% year-on-year from the second quarter's 12% growth.

"We continue to see healthy acquisition and retention trends on the membership side, and our recent price adjustments are going well on the pricing side," Netflix CFO Spencer Neumann said in response to questions on the company's last earnings call on the FX-neutral growth slowdown.

For the third quarter, Netflix is projecting adjusted EPS of $0.82 per share, in line with Wall Street estimates, and revenue of $12.86 billion against estimates of $12.88 billion, per CIQ data.

The recent merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery under the single moniker Skydance ( SKYD ) could present another challenge for Netflix, according to Needham analyst Laura Martin.

The newly formed Skydance boasts two historic movie studios, several major streaming networks, highly valuable IP such as "Harry Potter," and an annual content budget of $30 billion. That scale and content funding "threatens Netflix the most," Martin wrote.

Whereas Skydance is expected to have 30 wide-release films that will move to its streaming platforms in 2027, Netflix is only expected to have 12 limited-release films, per Needham estimates.

articles.title: Candy prices jump nearly 8%, but consumers are still willing to splurge this Halloween
articles.summary: Prices are higher, but it won't deter shoppers from leaning into the holidays.
articles.body:
Halloween's sweetest tradition is likely to cause a fright for consumers, with candy prices up nearly 8% from a year ago in the latest inflation report.

Candy and chewing gum prices increased by 7.7% last month, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' September Consumer Price Index , driven by higher cocoa prices. Overall inflation rose 3.7% in September, an acceleration from 3.4% in August.

Extreme weather in the Ivory Coast and Ghana quadrupled cocoa prices from January 2023 to January 2025. Manufacturers typically contract six months or even a year or two in advance, so Americans are paying higher prices now.

"After last year's record cocoa shortages and price spikes, the cocoa market is finally showing early signs of stabilizing, but not enough to deliver big price breaks for Halloween shoppers," David Branch of Wells Fargo said in a recent note.

Cocoa beans, sugar, and corn syrup represent roughly 65% of the ingredients in chocolate, per Branch. Sugar and sugar substitutes were up 5.5% year over year in the latest print.

Tariffs of 10% and 12.5% that took effect in July on 60 trading partners are adding to manufacturers' costs and are likely being passed along to consumers.

According to the National Retail Federation , shoppers plan to spend $13.5 billion in total this Halloween and $4.1 billion on candy alone.

"Consumers are faced with a lot of pressures. We have rising gas prices, inflation, and other things that are hitting their pocketbooks, but where they're not willing to pull back is on the things that matter to them and their families," NRF vice president of industry and consumer insights Allison Zeller told Yahoo Finance .

She added that shoppers are "spending a little bit more savvily."

Still, higher prices are driving frustration among Americans, with consumer sentiment near a record low . Gas and diesel have each set new record highs, heating oil costs are surging just ahead of winter, and housing costs show no signs of slowing.

To spread their budgets this Halloween, Zeller said many people are shopping for decor earlier and at various places, including online and even home improvement stores, to seek out deals.

At a conference in early September, Hershey ( HSY ) CEO Kirk Tanner said consumers have been "resilient" across income cohorts ahead of the key holiday season.

He said low-income consumers are "adapting" by going to convenience and dollar stores to look for lower-priced, smaller packs, while high-income consumers are buying larger packs in bulk, online, and at clubs, seeking out "more value from a price per ounce."

articles.title: The 2027 Social Security COLA is here: When will benefits increase?
articles.summary: Seniors will soon see one of the largest cost-of-living adjustments in years.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Retirees and those who receive Supplemental Security Income from the Social Security Administration now know just how much their benefits will increase next year.

The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, for its beneficiaries in 2027. It’s the largest hike in four years and one of the largest since 2000 .

On average, beneficiaries will see their monthly retirement benefits increase by about $75 a month, the SSA said.

The Social Security Administration’s annual COLAs are designed to help Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients retain their buying power amid rising inflation. These increases, which are issued annually, are determined using the Bureau of Labor’s Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which itself is a measure of the change in prices for common consumer goods and services.

The Labor Bureau actually releases a revised CPI-W each month, reflecting the change in prices concerning a number of consumer goods and services, including food, utilities and shelter. But only the data from July, August and September are considered when calculating the annual COLA adjustment for the following year.

This is the sixth consecutive year that the COLA has been at least 2.5%.

It won’t take effect for a few months, though.

The 3.6 percent increase will first impact your January benefits. For some, that payment will come in December.

The Social Security Administration follows a regular payment schedule for all of its beneficiaries. Payments may come earlier than expected if the intended disbursement date falls on a weekend or holiday.

Jan. 1, New Year’s Day, is considered a holiday, meaning the first 2027 payment for those who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will be paid on Dec. 31, 2026. The same is true for those who received Social Security before May 1997, or receive both Social Security and SSI.

Regardless of when your payment arrives, you will receive the full sum of your expected 2027 benefits.

articles.title: US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
articles.summary: Economists divided on Fed rate hike as inflation creates uncertainty before US midterm elections in a tense market.
articles.body:
United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.

Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.

Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.

“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.

Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.

In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”

Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.

Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.

At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.

Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.

“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.

The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years .

Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.

The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.

US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.

articles.title: India's WPI inflation surges to record high of 11.39% in September on higher food, fuel prices
articles.summary: India's wholesale price index (WPI)-based inflation surged to a series-high of 11.39% in September, up from 9.92% in August, driven by rising prices of
articles.body: India's wholesale price index (WPI)-based inflation surged to a series-high of 11.39% in September, up from 9.92% in August, driven by rising prices of food, manufactured items, and fuel and power, government data showed on Wednesday.Inflation in the food index rose to 8.66% in September from 7.05% in August. In manufactured items, wholesale inflation climbed to a series-high of 9.76%, compared with 8.37% in the previous month.Inflation in the fuel and power basket also accelerated, reaching 25.85% in September against 22.93% in August, according to data reported by news agency PTI.Why is wholesale inflation rising?Wholesale inflation has been on an upward trajectory since the beginning of the current financial year, with the West Asia war and the resulting blockade of the Strait of Hormuz pushing up global crude oil and fertiliser costs. The increase has also affected food and commodity prices.ICRA principal economist Rahul Agrawal said elevated global commodity inflation had pushed WPI inflation to a series high. Food inflation based on the WPI rose to a 23-month high in September 2026, amid a significant increase in inflation across cereals, pulses, fruits and vegetables.ICRA expects WPI inflation to rise further to 12% in October 2026, with higher food inflation, persistent global energy and commodity prices, and an adverse base effect contributing to the increase.Agrawal said wholesale inflation was expected to remain elevated in double digits through the third quarter of FY2027.Barclays also warned that wholesale and producer price inflation could accelerate in the coming months as international energy and metal prices remain elevated.“With international energy and metal prices elevated, wholesale and producer price inflation may accelerate in coming months,” Barclays said in a research note.The brokerage added that elevated global energy prices amid the Middle East conflict, alongside rising domestic food prices, were likely to push WPI inflation higher in the coming months.Producer prices and impact on businessesOutput producer price index (OPPI) inflation also rose to 11.4% year-on-year in September from 9.8% in August. The increase continued to be driven by higher manufacturing and mining producer price inflation, Barclays said.Industry chamber PHDCCI's Secretary General and CEO Ranjeet Mehta said the latest WPI figures pointed to inflationary pressures across several stages of production.While wholesale price movements do not translate directly into retail inflation, their persistence could affect corporate margins, working-capital requirements and investment decisions, Mehta said.Retail inflation also risesThe rise in wholesale inflation comes after retail inflation based on the consumer price index (CPI) climbed to 5.54% in September from 4.83% in August, reaching a 23-month high, according to government data reported earlier this week.September was the first month in which retail inflation crossed 5% under the new CPI series introduced earlier this year. The rate remained above the Reserve Bank of India's 4% target for the fourth consecutive month, although it was within the central bank's tolerance band of 2-6%.Food inflation under the CPI rose to 7.7% in September from 6% in August. Onions recorded a 108% year-on-year price rise, while garlic prices increased 55% and lemon prices rose 36%. Potato, tomato and lady finger prices, however, declined.Higher inflation in goods transport and restaurant services is at 14.7% and 9.4%, respectively, amid rising fuel costs.The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raised the benchmark policy rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% last week amid inflationary pressures.Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis said that the transmission of higher wholesale prices into consumer inflation was yet to be seen, adding that some industries, including durables, fast-moving consumer goods and automobiles, had announced price increases that could show up in the coming months.DBS Bank senior economist and executive director Radhika Rao said the RBI was expected to keep the possibility of another rate hike open at its December policy meeting.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump was trying to force prices lower ahead of the midterms. But Iran gets a vote, too
articles.summary: President Donald Trump and Republicans just got the worst news on inflation ahead of the midterms: Prices rose more than expected in September.
articles.body: President Donald Trump and Republicans just got the worst news on inflation ahead of the midterms: Prices rose more than expected in September. The news came as no surprise to American voters. Polls show they’re furious about the high cost of living that has persisted since the pandemic but has been exacerbated this year by Trump’s policies – including tariffs and, primarily, the Iran war. To alleviate some of the price pain, the Trump administration has been diving deep into its bag of tricks. Over a month ago, the US Navy began a high-stakes effort to assist tankers shuttling Gulf oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. And in a hail-Mary attempt, Trump last week announced a controversial deal to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. Iran and its Houthi allies are now undermining both of those operations. An increase in attacks on tankers and oil infrastructure over the past week has sent oil and diesel prices higher. The disruption has sent transits through the straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb falling sharply after mostly recovering to their pre-war levels. The Trump administration was never going to solve the inflation problem in the month leading up to the midterms. But its last-ditch effort for some positive news on prices has run face-first into a brick wall this week. Inflation Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index showed a familiar story: Inflation continued to rise in September, boosted mostly by surging energy costs. Gas prices rose 9.1% over the course of the month and ended September more than 34% higher than the same time last year. Fuel oil prices rose 15.3% last month and surged more than 74% over the course of the past year. Those higher costs are starting to spread to other parts of the economy. As my colleague Matt Egan noted Tuesday, the Iran war is costing the average American household $2,000 in additional costs, according to Moody’s Analytics. Particularly concerning in Wednesday’s inflation report was the surprising rebound in housing and rent costs, a significant contributor to inflation that had cooled off in the spring and summer. All services rose 0.4% in the month – prices that tend to rise as yoga studios, lawn services and the like charge their customers more to make up for their rising costs. Those services prices may only be a knock-on effect from the Iran war, but economists get worried when they rise, because they tend to be “sticky.” Bluntly: When was the last time your kids’ nursery school lowered prices? The overall US economy remains hot and consumers keep spending despite rising prices. But higher inflation has translated into higher bond yields and rates from the Federal Reserve, which are lifting borrowing costs and making housing even less affordable. The Strait of Hormuz Iran knows all this. It knows the political pressure Trump and his Republican party are facing. And it knows what month it is. After a relatively quiet September, at least 18 vessels in and around the Middle East have been attacked over the past two weeks, according to Kpler, a maritime tracking service. On Tuesday, the Iran-allied Houthis appeared to hit the headquarters of Saudi state oil giant Aramco. “It appears Iran is attempting to keep oil prices high ahead of the midterm elections, and the best way to do this has been to increase attacks - both from themselves and via the Houthis,” said Matt Smith, analyst at Kpler. The ever-shifting narrative about who controls the Strait of Hormuz has changed once again. The complex operation of naval-protected dark fleets shuttling Gulf oil out of the strait and offloading it to tankers in the Gulf of Oman had been hugely successful. Just a few weeks ago, oil transits out of the Strait of Hormuz had almost fully recovered to their pre-war levels. Over the past seven days, oil and fuel transits through the strait have fallen to 54% of their pre-war levels, according to Kpler. Iran’s retaliation should surprise no one, said Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners. “As the US trumpets the success of getting more crude out to global markets, it feels somewhat like sporting a big ‘kick me’ sign,” he said. “Iran is attacking almost everyone. Meanwhile, Iran’s proxy, the Houthis, are attacking Saudi Arabia with substantial results.” Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure have raised the stakes of the war. Although the oil market largely dodged a bullet after a successful but repairable attack on Saudi Arabia’s crucial East-West pipeline, the recent attacks prove that the conflict isn’t abating anytime soon. The ultimate winner can’t yet be known: The US Navy may once again gain the upper hand. The administration may find other creative ways to get more diesel flowing to the market. In the meantime, the loser is clear: The American consumer. And in three weeks they will be casting their verdict on the economy as they vote in the midterms.

articles.title: Canara Bank Q2 net profit rises 8.4% to Rs 5,175 cr; biz crosses Rs 30 lakh cr
articles.summary: Canara Bank Q2 net profit rises 8.4% to Rs 5,175 crore as business crosses Rs 30.7 lakh crore; NII hits Rs 11,000 crore, NPAs fall.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Canara Bank’s net profit rose 8.4% year on year to Rs 5,175 crore in the September quarter, while global business grew 15.8% to Rs 30.7 lakh crore, driven by strong credit growth and higher core income.“We have crossed a significant milestone of Rs 30 lakh crore in total business. Net interest income grew 20.3% to an all-time high of around Rs 11,000 crore, and we recorded our highest-ever quarterly profit in absolute terms,” said Brajesh Kumar Singh, managing director and CEO of Canara Bank.Global advances grew 19.4% year on year to Rs 13.7 lakh crore, while global deposits rose 13.1% to Rs 16.9 lakh crore. Domestic advances increased 16.9% to Rs 12.6 lakh crore, and domestic deposits grew 10.9% to Rs 15.4 lakh crore.Retail lending expanded 31.61% to Rs 3.3 lakh crore. Housing loans grew 17.3% to Rs 1.3 lakh crore, while overall retail, agriculture and MSME (RAM) credit increased 21% to Rs 8.1 lakh crore. Vehicle loans grew more than 25%.“We have a pipeline of around Rs 50,000 crore in large corporate lending, which should materialise this quarter. With the festive season driving retail demand and consumption, I expect the quarter to be good,” Singh said.Asset quality improved, with the gross non-performing assets (GNPA) ratio declining to 1.33% in the Sept quarter from 2.3% a year earlier. The net NPA ratio fell to 0.30% from 0.54%. The provision coverage ratio improved to 95.34%.“Our guidance was to bring gross NPA down to 1.5% by March next year. articles.title: Tesla's Roadster event is back on for Thursday night. Here's what to expect.
articles.summary: After a two-week delay, the Tesla Roadster event is back on — for now.
articles.body:
After a two-week delay, the Tesla ( TSLA ) Roadster event is back on — for now.

This week, Tesla added a countdown clock to its Tesla Roadster website , stating that the reveal would occur at 7:55 p.m. CDT on Oct. 15, two weeks after the initial Oct. 1 reveal date. Tesla said the reveal was pushed back due to weather conditions at the demo site, SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Rocket Development and Testing facility in Waco, Texas . The event will be streamed on Tesla's X account .

Stormy weather would've likely hampered the Roadster's rumored hovering or flying ability. The Information reported several weeks ago that the reveal event on Oct. 1 could include a demonstration of a limited-edition version of the Roadster equipped with cold-gas thrusters developed in collaboration with SpaceX ( SPCX ), possibly including airborne flight.

Tesla is asking prospective buyers to put down a $5,000 deposit, followed by a $45,000 wire transfer due within 10 days of the initial deposit.

Tesla has not said how much the new Roadster will cost, though it is expected to exceed $250,000. However, when Tesla announced the 7:55 p.m. CDT reveal time on X.com, CEO Elon Musk replied, "Timing is everything," suggesting the digits may have some meaning.

Longtime analyst and Tesla bull Pierre Ferragu suggested it could have something to do with the price, then coyly threw out the number $75,990. He later followed up with the idea that the Roadster event should start at "7:59:90." Some have suggested this could refer to the starting price of the car's base model or to a particular track time the Roadster achieved.

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever EV and used a Lotus Elise chassis.

Tesla announced its successor way back in 2017, took in reservations with those high deposits, and originally said deliveries would begin in 2020. Those initial reservation holders have been waiting for quite a long time.

During his appearance on the All-In Summit , Musk brought up the Tesla Roadster.

"It'll be a banger. Excitement guaranteed. Success is not guaranteed, but excitement is," he added, with All-In host Jason Calacanis claiming he had seen a preview of the event, and that the demo would "blow people's minds."

articles.title: He inherited land from mother, redeveloped home & received Rs 75 lakh from builder; taxman denied capital gains exemption, but ITAT Delhi gives relief, ruling multiple floors can qualify as one house
articles.summary: You give your house for redevelopment to a builder and get money from the builder and some floors.
articles.body: You give your house for redevelopment to a builder and get money from the builder and some floors. You claim long-term capital gains exemption, but the tax department sends you a notice for what it sees as multiple residential units. What do you do?In one such case, a man in Delhi, received Rs 75 lakh from the builder and faced a tax notice. Let’s understand why and how he managed to win relief with the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Delhi.What the case is aboutA man inherited 400 square yards of leasehold land from his late mother in 1997. He subsequently initiated the process of converting the land into freehold. In 1998, Delhi Development Authority (DDA) transferred the property's records into his name through mutation.Also Read | He gave up his land for road widening and got TDRs which he sold for Rs 6.02 crore to a builder; landowner gets tax notice, ITAT rules proceeds taxable as capital gains but allows land cost deductionThe conversion was completed by 1999, making him the owner of the freehold property. His mother had constructed a single-storey house on the plot in 1978, but the son decided to redevelop it. Towards the end of 1999, he entered into an agreement with a developer to demolish the existing house and construct a new building.Under the arrangement, the man retained the rights to the basement, ground floor, second floor and the open terrace that was above the second floor. As per the agreement, the builder was entitled to the entire first floor of the building. The first floor was subsequently divided and sold as three separate units to three people.Nearly two decades later, in 2018, the man along with the other three people who had ownership of the first floor decided to undertake another redevelopment of the property. They entered into a fresh agreement with another builder, under which the existing building was to be demolished and replaced with a new structure.The agreement specified how ownership rights would be distributed after reconstruction. The was to receive the basement, the entire ground floor, the entire third floor and the open terrace. The builder was allocated the whole second floor, while the first floor remained with the three people, according to an ET report.Also Read | She worked as a teacher till 62 years of age instead of retiring at 60, but was denied gratuity because of extended service; Allahabad HC orders payment with 6% interestAs part of the 2018 redevelopment agreement, the man received Rs 75 lakh from the builder. Each of the three first-floor owners received Rs 25 lakh. The man, however, did not pay income tax on the transaction, claiming an exemption under Section 54 for long-term capital gains on the entire portion of the building allotted to him, comprising the ground floor, basement and third floor.The Income Tax Officer (AO) rejected the man’s claim and concluded that he was liable to pay tax.The man challenged the decision and secured a favourable ruling from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Delhi, on July 13, 2026.Why did the son win the case and pay no tax?Chartered Accountant Suresh Surana told ET that the Delhi ITAT had to examine whether the basement, ground floor and third floor allotted to the man under the new redevelopment agreement could be treated as separate residential houses for claiming long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax exemption under Section 54.The tribunal also considered whether the Income Tax Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting the property's fair market value determined through reports prepared by registered valuers.Also Read | Man enters JDA for land, gets 6 flats from builder and transfers 5 to wife, but gets tax notice; ITAT Delhi deletes Rs 4.14 crore additions after finding no stock-in-trade conversion or saleUnder the 2018 redevelopment agreement, the man received Rs 75 lakh and declared the capital gains arising from the transaction. He subsequently claimed an exemption under Sections 54/54F in respect of the basement, ground floor and third floor allotted to him.The man calculated the property's value using the fair market value of the inherited land as on April 1, 2001, supported by reports from registered valuers to come up with the value of the capital gains.The Assessing Officer was not in agreement with this approach and on his part classified the basement, ground floor and third floor as three separate residential units. The officer's reasoning was that the portions were physically distinct and could be used independently.The officer also relied on the amendment to Section 54 introduced in the Union Budget 2025, which restricted the exemption to one residential house. Applying this amendment, the Assessing Officer permitted the man to claim the capital gains tax exemption for only the ground floor.The dispute also extended to the valuation of the inherited property. The Assessing Officer rejected the fair market value adopted by the owner and replaced it with a lower value derived from government sources. However, the officer did so without referring the matter to the Departmental Valuation Officer (DVO) for examination of the valuation difference.The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), or CIT(A), upheld the Assessing Officer's findings. The appellate authority also did not take into account the builder's certificate submitted as evidence of the actual construction cost.Also Read | He bought a diesel SUV for Rs 13.69 lakh; but repeated DPF issues followed; consumer commission finds deficiency in service and awards Rs 10.99 lakh refund, 9% interest and compensationThe Delhi ITAT held that the presence of several floors or portions that are capable of independent use within one building does not automatically mean that a taxpayer has acquired multiple residential houses.It observed that dividing a residential building vertically or according to its intended use is simply a way of organising the property to meet current or even future requirements.The tribunal also relied primarily on the Delhi High Court's ruling in Pr. CIT v. Lata Goel. The decision clarified that acquiring more than one floor within the same residential property does not, by itself, mean you have acquired multiple residential houses.According to Surana, separate entrances, kitchens and bathrooms on different floors, or the ability to use each portion independently, were not sufficient grounds on their own to deny the man income tax exemption under Section 54/54F.The restriction introduced after the 2015 amendment, which refers to investment in “one residential house”, applies to the acquisition of multiple separate houses. It does not require the eligible residential property to consist of only one floor or a single self-contained unit.On this basis, Jain was entitled to claim the Section 54 exemption from long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax for the basement, ground floor and third floor of the same residential building.The tribunal also held that the Assessing Officer could not discard the valuation reports prepared by registered valuers and replace their estimates with an arbitrary figure without pointing out specific deficiencies in the reports or referring the matter to the Departmental Valuation Officer.Another important piece of evidence was the builder's certificate dated February 7, 2023. According to Surana, the document recorded a construction cost of Rs 2.54 crore for the portions handed over to the man. This figure had a direct bearing on the computation of capital gains.The ITAT observed that the CIT(A) had wrongly disregarded the certificate despite its relevance to the case.These findings ultimately led to the man’s victory before the Delhi ITAT. After examining the construction cost, the registered valuers' reports and his claim for LTCG tax exemption under Section 54, the tribunal directed the Assessing Officer to recalculate the capital gains in accordance with the man’s computations, as set out in the order. The revised calculation resulted in no taxable long-term capital gain.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tehran municipality accused of ‘overstep’ after launching welfare projects
articles.summary: Tehran’s new municipal welfare projects face intense criticism over funding sources, transparency, and inflation claims.
articles.body:
Tehran municipality has launched a series of welfare initiatives to help residents cope with soaring living costs, but the measures have raised questions about their financing and effectiveness, as well as whether the local authority is taking on responsibilities better handled by Iran’s national government.

The local authority has launched four projects it says are aimed at protecting citizens, including a housing project, freezes on the prices of 12 basic goods , and a maternity package.

Questions have been raised about how they will be funded and whether the municipality is overstepping its traditional functions.

In Iran, municipalities are responsible for local services and urban management, while the national government oversees broader economic policy, including efforts to control inflation.

Iranian law does give municipalities some responsibilites beyond conventional urban services, but Article 55 of Iran’s Municipal Law does call for municipalities to provide for public food markets, make certain essential goods more affordable, and provide social welfare facilities and low-cost housing.

The dispute is therefore less about whether Tehran municipality can provide the services, and more about their scale and financing.

The municipality’s price-freezing initiative, dubbed the “Zero Inflation” project, has been the most controversial. It comes as year-on-year inflation reached nearly 90 percent last month, while annual food inflation hit 108.8 percent.

Doubts have been raised about how the project will be funded and its effectiveness. Others believe that the measures could fuel inequality between the capital and other cities.

They are viewed as steps to address the huge economic challenges faced by Tehran residents, worsened since the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28.

Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani said the municipality had recently guaranteed prices ranging between 5 percent and 50 percent below market rates for the next six months.

Yousef Akandeh, a political activist, told Al Jazeera that freezing the prices of some goods or providing free services will not reduce inflation to zero alone.

“Even if we assume that the Tehran municipality succeeded in stabilising the prices of 12 basic goods, what about the rise in rents, medicines, transportation prices, and the rest of living expenses,” Akandeh asked.

Real steps to tackle inflation, Akandeh said, would have to begin with controlling liquidity growth and monetary discipline, which he said are nearly impossible amid the ongoing war.

The municipality has also introduced a maternity support programme offering mothers of children born this year monthly credits worth up to 40 million rials ($15) for two years for each newborn.

Akandeh raised the issue of institutional overlap, noting that a similar national scheme already exists.

“The government implements a similar package and provides monthly financial amounts for all newborns across the country and not just in Tehran, and if the municipality’s package is independent of it, the Tehrani family may benefit from the national and municipal programme simultaneously,” Akandeh said.

Receiving support from both programmes would not, in itself, indicate wrongdoing. But critics are instead raising the question of whether it is an appropriate use of Tehran’s municipal resources, particularly when the city faces competing spending demands.

Amir Dabiri Mehr, a former adviser in the Tehran municipality, told Al Jazeera that although supporting the homeless falls under the municipality’s social responsibilities, the problem lies in a lack of transparency. The municipality is funded by taxes and building density licences.

“The people have the right to know what the municipality spends within the framework of its original tasks, and in tasks it has chosen for itself, and where it gets its resources from?” Dabiri Mehr said.

The municipality-affiliated Hamshahri newspaper said that the “Zero Inflation” project is not funded by municipal budget subsidies, but through direct purchases from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in council-run stores.

The biggest crisis facing Tehran’s residents is housing, which is the national government’s responsibility, Mehr said. Food and living expenses are the national government’s responsibility.

“If the goal is to solve the people’s problems, it seems that the biggest problem facing the residents of Tehran today is the housing crisis, and this dilemma cannot be solved by building an apartment building consisting of a few residential units,” he said.

Al Jazeera attempted to contact the Tehran municipality for comment but received no response.

Tehran Mayor Zakani has, however, defended the financing arrangements, telling a local newspaper, Hamshahri, that the Zero Inflation initiative would not rely on direct subsidies from the municipal budget, but instead on purchasing goods directly from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in city-run stores.

Zakani also said that the programme would draw on municipal resources, bank financing, and partnerships.

articles.title: Netflix laying off 6 percent of its workforce, marking biggest round of job cuts in years
articles.summary: Netflix’s product, tech, legal and human resources teams would be the most impacted, according to a memo from co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos.
articles.body:
(AP) — Netflix plans to lay off about 6 percent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the streaming giant makes wider “organizational changes.”

Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos announced the job cuts in a memo to employees Wednesday. They said the company’s product, tech, legal and human resources teams would be the most impacted.

“Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly,” Peters and Sarandos wrote in the memo, which was obtained by The Associated Press. They maintained business was strong — but that Netflix needed to be “disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources” as it invests in future growth and “high impact areas to improve our service.”

Beyond the memo from its chief executives, the streaming company declined to comment further about Wednesday’s cuts.

Between membership signups and price increases, Netflix’s profit has grown this year. In its second financial quarter , the company earned $3.4 billion and racked up revenue of $12.56 billion — up 9 percent and 13 percent, respectively, from the same period last year.

Still, the company’s forecast for the third quarter fell below Wall Street’s expectations. The company plans to report those earnings next week.

Competition in the streaming space is growing more crowded overall. Netflix continues to be a dominant player (accounting for 19 percent of the market per the latest data from streaming guide JustWatch), but rivals like Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+ are close behind.

HBO Max and Paramount+ are also now under the same roof — Skydance — after Paramount’s $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery closed last week. The new Hollywood giant plans to unify its streaming products “into a single service over time.” Netflix initially inked a deal to buy Warner’s studio and streaming business late last year but walked away from that offer back in February.

At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The layoffs announced Wednesday mark the biggest round of cuts the California-based company has rolled out in years.

The Wall Street Journal first reported Wednesday’s news of the layoffs.

articles.title: Under 30 and think you'll never own a home? Here's what a star housing strategist recommends.
articles.summary: Meredith Whitney, who predicted the housing meltdown, offers advice to young would-be homeowners who feel priced out of the market.
articles.body:
For young people seeking the American dream through homeownership, the best option at this point may be to buy a major fixer-upper in a less-than-perfect neighborhood.

"Well, one thing that's going on within the housing market is you're seeing — and this is also with the 21st Century housing bill that passed just several months ago — is you're going into blighted areas and investing in the rehabilitation of those homes. And that's actually a much cheaper way of owning a home than otherwise," Meredith Whitney, CEO of Meredith Whitney Advisory Group, said on Sozzi Unleashed .

"Detroit's the perfect example of this," she continued, "where you had an economic revival with blighted areas, with run-down areas and investment in those areas. You can get a home for a massive discount to what you would have in the more established areas. And these areas are getting also economic investment from corporations. And you're seeing real revival."

Whitney is credited with spotting the housing market meltdown more than a decade ago as a star Wall Street analyst.

"Young people are supposed to be, you know, risk takers, [so doing that] would make a lot out of sense," she added. "And there are still urban areas. So there's still where they want to be. Young people want to be in urban areas. This is just a different take on it."

The realities facing many would-be young homebuyers are stark amid sky-high mortgage rates and rising costs of home ownership and maintenance.

About 9 in 10 adults younger than 40 say it's harder for young adults today to buy a home than it was for their parents' generation, according to a new Pew Research Center survey.

Since 2019, home prices in the US have risen faster than young adults' incomes, according to the Pew Research data.

Between 2019 and 2024, the inflation-adjusted median home value rose 30%, Pew noted, while the inflation-adjusted median household income for households headed by those under 40 rose only 9%.

Whitney thinks the challenges facing housing will persist for some time to come.

articles.title: Deep-tech needs more repeat entrepreneurs: TDK Ventures chief Sauvage
articles.summary: India needs more patient and corporate venture capital for deep-tech as long gestation cycles limit repeat founders, says TDK Ventures chief Nicolas Sauvage.
articles.body: Bengaluru: India needs more patient capital and corporate venture capital to build globally competitive deep-tech companies, as the sector’s long gestation periods and limited pool of repeat entrepreneurs make it fundamentally different from software-as-a-service (SaaS) and fintech, said Nicolas Sauvage, president of TDK Ventures.TDK Ventures manages $500 million across four funds and has 56 portfolio companies globally. India is its second-largest market by number of investments, with six completed investments and a seventh in the pipeline, Sauvage said.“Overnight success takes 10 years. I think that is particularly true of deep tech,” he said, pointing to the difference in investment horizons between software businesses and ventures involving semiconductors, energy storage, robotics and space.While SaaS and fintech companies can generate exits in four to five years, deep-tech businesses may take six to eight years or longer to mature, de-risk their technology and establish a market. This also slows the emergence of repeat entrepreneurs who can draw on their experience to build successive companies.“If you have an exit in SaaS every four years, you have successful entrepreneurs who can start another company and start another one. In deep tech, you may have that cycle only once every 10 years,” he said.TDK Ventures’ current Indian portfolio includes electric two-wheeler maker Ultraviolette Automotive; Exponent Energy, which focuses on electrifying heavy mobility, including buses and trucks; C2i Semiconductors, which enables efficient power delivery within GPU racks; EtherealX, which focuses on commercial space technology and fully reusable medium-lift launch vehicles; and agritech firm Fasal.India is still largely in the first cycle of deep-tech entrepreneurship, unlike the US, where successful companies have spawned networks of experienced founders. Sauvage cited the “Tesla mafia” as an example, saying TDK Ventures had invested in six companies founded by former Tesla employees.TDK portfolio company Exponent Energy illustrates how Indian market conditions can create an advantage for deep-tech startups. It began by developing battery-management systems for electric three-wheelers, targeting a fragmented market of more than 70 manufacturers that could not necessarily develop the technology in-house.Having matured its technology in India, the company has moved towards fast-charging electric buses, with potential applications in overseas markets, including Europe.TDK Ventures is looking at opportunities across computing, semiconductors, energy transition, thermal batteries, heat pumps, mobility, agriculture and space. Its investment philosophy requires each portfolio company to have the potential to return the entire fund, while also delivering strategic value and contributing positively to society and the planet.Sauvage said conventional fund structures could constrain deep-tech investing because they require investors to exit or distribute holdings within finite periods.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump adviser sees ‘a whole bunch of good news’ in inflation report
articles.summary: Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), said Wednesday he sees a “bunch of good news” in the latest inflation report, which measured prices as up 3.7 percent year over year in September. Speaking to NewsNation’s Hannah Brandt at the White House, Hassett said the latest consumer price index (CPI) showed a…
articles.body:
Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council (NEC), said Wednesday he sees a “bunch of good news” in the latest inflation report , which measured prices as up 3.7 percent year over year in September.

Speaking to NewsNation’s Hannah Brandt at the White House, Hassett said the latest consumer price index (CPI) showed a “surge in energy prices,” which he deemed “temporary.”

Annual inflation rose from 3.4 percent in August to 3.7 percent last month, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Energy prices also spiked by 5.2 percent from August to September and were up by 20.4 percent year over year.

“But there’s a whole bunch of good news in the report,” Hassett told Brandt.

The NEC director noted that food prices held steady from August to September, while the price of prescription drugs fell by 1.2 percent.

President Trump has touted his administration’s direct-to-consumer drug platform , TrumpRx, which launched earlier this year .

“My expectation is that the strength of all the things that we’ve been doing in terms of getting food prices down and getting drug prices down, that strength is going to motor through,” Hassett remarked.

CPI inflation in September reached its highest point since May , when prices were up 4.2 percent year over year. Core annual inflation, which does not include more volatile food and energy prices, was also 2.6 percent last month — up from 2.4 percent in August.

The 9.1 percent monthly increase in gas prices accounted for more than half of the monthly rise in prices, the BLS reported. Gas and diesel cost more than $4 and $6 per gallon on average, respectively, amid the ongoing Iran war.

Matthew Middleton, a spokesperson for the White House, told NewsNation that Trump “has always been clear about temporary disruptions” from the Iran war.

Trump has argued higher prices at the pump are worth it for the U.S. military to eliminate Iran’s nuclear capabilities.

“While Democrats pretend to care about ‘affordability’ this administration has delivered tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families,” Middleton added, referencing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and job growth under Trump.

Hassett also blamed the Biden administration, telling Brandt that Americans “were worse off” due to the former president’s policies.

But inflation in December 2024, Biden’s final full month in office, was 2.9 percent. Inflation reached a 40-year high in June 2022, reaching 9.1 percent, as measured by the CPI.

Real average hourly earnings last month were down 0.5 percent from August, the BLS reported , as inflation outpaced wage growth.

Heather Long, the chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said Wednesday the latest inflation data was “painful” and showed inflation is “a lot more broad-based and entrenched” in the economy than what economists thought.

“It was a tough report all around,” Long told The Hill. “The more that you look through the details, the more troubling it became.”
