articles.title: US stocks fall as inflation accelerates; S&P 500 drops 1.1%, Nasdaq slides 1.6%
articles.summary: Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher, adding to concerns about borrowing costs
articles.body: Wall Street stocks fell on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher, adding to concerns about borrowing costs even as major banks assessed the opportunities and risks associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom.The S&P 500 fell 1.1%, putting it on track for its fifth decline in six sessions since hitting a record high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 171 points, or 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite declined 1.6%, as of 1:14 pm Eastern time.US consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August and exceeding economists’ expectations of 3.6%. The data fuelled concerns that inflation could remain elevated, partly due to rising energy prices amid the war with Iran.The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield climbed to 5.23%, after briefly crossing 5.32% during the session. Higher yields can weigh on equities by increasing borrowing costs and making bonds more attractive relative to stocks.Meanwhile, executives at major US banks highlighted the opportunities presented by AI infrastructure investment, while cautioning that uncertainty over demand, financing costs and returns could create risks.Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon said the long-term demand for capital and computing capacity required by the AI ecosystem remained uncertain.“No one knows how the demands for capital and compute will evolve as the broader AI ecosystem matures,” Solomon said, stressing the need for vigilance in financing decisions and risk management.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, however, said investment in the broader AI ecosystem was not slowing, citing an ongoing shortage of computing capacity.The AI infrastructure expansion, driven by heavy investment in data centres and computing power, presents banks with opportunities to finance large-scale projects. However, elevated interest rates could raise project costs, squeeze returns and make debt repayment more difficult.Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf described the AI buildout as a significant economic force, bringing both opportunities and risks because of the substantial borrowing involved and pressure on prices across some industries and supply chains.Banks are also deploying AI internally to improve productivity and reduce costs, although the financial benefits vary. Fraser said Citi was developing products up to 40% faster using AI and had reduced technology vendor expenses by 30% through coding tools.Investors are watching whether such efficiency gains can justify the heavy spending on AI. Concerns are also mounting over cybersecurity threats and the risks posed by AI agents capable of taking actions autonomously.The combination of persistent inflation, elevated bond yields and uncertainty over AI investment returns has added to the challenges facing Wall Street, where high stock valuations leave limited room for corporate earnings or productivity gains to disappoint.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Yikes': CoreWeave stock tanks on bond yield woes, CEO blames market 'irrationally'
articles.summary: CoreWeave stock fell more than 16% in morning trading on Wednesday, a day after a chart of its rising borrowing costs drew a one-word reply from Elon Musk: "...
articles.body:
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock fell more than 16% on Wednesday, a day after a chart of its rising borrowing costs gained traction on X.

Bloomberg, citing an internal memo, reports that the AI cloud company's CEO stated in a memo that the market is acting "irrationally."

"When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," CEO Mike Intrator wrote to staff. "We are confident in our business model, our customers, the extraordinary quality of our execution, and the relentless discipline around the financial engine we have built."

A bond's yield rises as its price falls, so a yield near 15% means investors want a steep return to lend CoreWeave money.

Intrator added that "factors like the weakness and delays surrounding the attempted IPOs and debt financings" of several CoreWeave rivals "are bleeding into the narrative around CoreWeave."

On Tuesday, venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya posted a chart showing that the yield on $1.25 billion of CoreWeave bonds due in 2032 "touched 15% today, then closed at a new high" of 14.5%.

"Is the AI buildout creating a private credit bubble?" Palihapitiya asked.

Musk, who owns the platform, replied with one word: " Yikes ."

The selling spread to other AI cloud stocks: Nebius ( NBIS ) fell 11%, Oracle ( ORCL ) dropped another 9%, and the following stocks sank more than 10%: DigitalOcean ( DOCN ), Hut 8 ( HUT ), Cipher ( CIFR ), TeraWulf ( WULF ), and IREN ( IREN ).

CoreWeave rents out Nvidia ( NVDA ) chips to AI companies and pays for much of that hardware with debt. The company's interest expense rose to $640 million in the second quarter from $267 million a year earlier, and it lost $626 million in the quarter, according to Yahoo Finance data. Revenue more than doubled over the same stretch to $2.58 billion.

Total debt reached about $52 billion at the end of June, up from about $15 billion a year earlier.

The company is clearly looking for cheaper money. CoreWeave is chasing insurers' vast pools of capital to fund its build-out, the Financial Times reported Wednesday.

Co-founder Brannin McBee, who leads CoreWeave's financing, told the FT that investment-grade ratings on more of its chip-backed debt would let it borrow from insurers, whose capital "is unlimited. Like, that's all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche."

McBee said CoreWeave will keep taking out chip-backed loans: "I don't look at that as scary debt at all. I look at that as accelerating debt and great debt."

articles.summary: Stocks wobbled as the third quarter earnings season got underway and investors digested fresh inflation data.
articles.body: Stocks declined to session lows in afternoon trading on Wednesday as investors digested hotter-than-expected inflation data, and bank earnings continued to roll in.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) slipped 0.4% while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 1.3%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 2% after stocks staggered lower on Tuesday.September's Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7% year over year, versus 3.6% expected by economists. Higher gas and energy prices drove inflation higher, lowering the odds that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady at its next policy meeting. Semiconductor stocks continued to sell off after the KOSPI index (^KS11) declined 12% over the past five days. Chip equipment maker ASML (ASML) on Wednesday posted record third quarter sales and raised its full-year outlook amid strong AI demand. Investors await Taiwan Semiconductor earnings on Thursday (TSM) for further confirmation of the AI boom. Elsewhere, the parade of financial company earnings continued with results from Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS). Bank of America stock sank as much as 9% as a $1.2 billion regulatory penalty and a slowdown in its Wall Street machine dented lending income. Meanwhile, BlackRock (BLK) shares rose after third quarter earnings beat analyst expectations. The results round out third quarter reporting among Wall Street's biggest banks, which have indicated consumers are holding up despite higher interest rates, among other signals.Separately, Apple's (AAPL) market capitalization once again crossed the $5 trillion mark in intraday trading, just months after it first touched the threshold in late July.Brent crude futures (BZ=F), the global benchmark, remained above $105 per barrel as Houthis continued to bomb Saudi Arabian energy facilities.
